title: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package of 'everyday fixes'
titleJa: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package of 'everyday fixes'
summaryJa: The chancellor will axe tariffs on some staples as part of plans to give households "breathing space".
bodyOriginal:
Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package of 'everyday fixes'
- Published
John Healey will remove import taxes on marmalade, gherkins and more than 100 products in a bid to give families "breathing space" with the cost of living at the Budget.
The chancellor on Wednesday will promise a fresh series of "everyday fixes" to ease the pressure on households.
The measures will also include an end to the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments and higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent.
But the Conservatives said the offer of "cheaper gherkins" was "an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises".
Ahead of the Budget, the government said it is removing tariffs on more than 100 "family favourite" products, while supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser costs and households reliant on heating oil.
The government says the changes could save households up to £21 per year when combined with existing tariff suspensions on products including pasta, fruit juice and tuna.
Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
- Published22 hours ago
Marmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional £19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.
Healey said the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine had "hit families here at home through higher everyday costs".
"We can't control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference," he added.
Other measures the government announced include:
Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that
Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead
Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period
And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn't mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren't fair.
"If you're a nurse driving for work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket."
But the Conservatives said Burnham's "everyday fixes" have already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.
Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

title: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
titleJa: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
summaryJa: Comey for years has been targeted by President Donald Trump, who fired him as FBI director in 2017.
bodyOriginal:
Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for the third time with federal crimes, according to a court filing unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., at Comey's request.
Comey is accused in the new case with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it.
He is also charged with conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information.
The charging document, known as an information, says Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed individual "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication."
According to a court filing by Comey, who is seeking to dismiss the new case, the information relates to the "alleged disclosure of classified information" to The New York Times on Oct. 5, 2016.
Comey's lawyers told a judge in that filing that the alleged disclosure "was investigated by two separate U.S. Attorneys over the past ten years. Both declined to prosecute."
Comey has been repeatedly targeted by the Department of Justice under the administration of President Donald Trump, who fired him as FBI director in 2017. Both men have been fierce critics of one another since then.
The DOJ filed the information against Comey on Oct. 5 and asked a judge to seal it, citing the risk that an ongoing criminal investigation would be compromised by the charges becoming public. Judge Trevor McFadden granted that request that day.
Attorneys for Comey, whom the DOJ agreed should be notified of the information, filed a motion to dismiss the case on Oct. 9, arguing that the 10-year statute of limitations to file a grand jury indictment relating to events of Oct. 5, 2016, had expired.
Comey's lawyers accused the DOJ of filing "a faulty information under seal" in an effort to put the statute of limitations on hold.
The attorneys on Monday asked McFadden to unseal the information, and the judge agreed to do so.
Comey separately is currently seeking the dismissal of an indictment obtained by the DOJ in North Carolina federal court on charges of threatening Trump's life by posting a photo of seashells on a beach on social media. He previously successfully won dismissal of another indictment accusing him of falsely testifying to Congress.
The new criminal complaint came to light hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the Department of Justice had unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, last year as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
"Well, they're back — again," James Comey said in a video message on Substack addressing the new case.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
"And I'm still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this," Comey said. "The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."
In the pending indictment in North Carolina, Comey in late April was charged with threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
Prosecutors claim that the number "86" — which is often used in restaurants to indicate a menu item is no longer available — was code for suggesting someone kill Trump, who is the 47th U.S. president.
Comey has denied any wrongdoing in that case and is seeking to have the indictment tossed out by a judge.
Comey was first indicted in September 2025 by a federal grand jury in Virginia on charges of making a false statement and obstruction, in connection with testimony he gave before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 30, 2020.
Comey, in that testimony, denied authorizing another person at the FBI to serve as an anonymous source in news reports regarding an investigation of Hillary Clinton and her emails when she was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016.
That first indictment was dismissed by a judge on Nov. 24, 2025, after the judge ruled that Lindsey Halligan, a then-interim U.S. attorney who obtained the indictments, had been invalidly appointed.
On the same day the judge tossed Comey's case for that reason, the same judge dismissed an unrelated indictment obtained by Halligan against New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had been accused of bank fraud and making false statements to a financial institution in connection with a home mortgage she obtained in 2020.
James, like Comey, has been a staunch critic of Trump, and a target of the president's ire.

title: JetBlue posts bigger loss on fuel costs, but CEO says margins improving
titleJa: JetBlue posts bigger loss on fuel costs, but CEO says margins improving
summaryJa: JetBlue Airways is in the middle of a plan that aims to cut costs and increase premium revenue.
bodyOriginal:
JetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but the New York carrier said strong travel demand is helping to offset higher fuel prices as it seeks to calm investors after shares fell to a new low Monday.
JetBlue stock soared roughly 11% in after-hours trading Monday.
JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million.
"Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected," CEO Joanna Geraghty said in an earnings release. "That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity."
JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.
JetBlue executives are set to hold an earnings call on Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET, where they will face questions from analysts about the company's long-term health amid sustained losses. A group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.
The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.
JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday.
"Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."
Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expected
- Revenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expected
JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.
Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares, which are up more than 20% this year.
JetBlue has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals.
It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines.

title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push
titleJa: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push
summaryJa: Microsoft is trying to balance a rapid AI infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
bodyOriginal:
Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below.
Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.
Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. Capital expenditures for the September quarter should exceed $50 billion, Microsoft said in July. In the same quarter a year ago, capital spending and finance leases came to $34.9 billion.
That's put a strain on Microsoft's finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees.
"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program."
Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation, increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use. It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results. At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.
The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile. In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.
Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added.
More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July. But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.
On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.

title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
titleJa: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
summaryJa: Anthropic’s IPO prospectus is 355 pages and full of never before disclosed company information.
bodyOriginal:
Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
- Published
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.
The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.
Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.
Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.
1. Armageddon is an occupational hazard
Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.
Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.
"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.
It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.
But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".
One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.
2. The company is haemorrhaging cash
Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.
The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.
Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.
The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.
Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.
Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.
"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.
3. But luckily it has plenty of cash on hand
Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.
At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.
Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.
Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.
The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.
Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.
Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.
4. Anthropic relies on a few big customers
Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.
A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.
An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.
Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".
The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.
Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.
Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.
Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".
The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.
5. AI promises 'extraordinary' benefits to the world
For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.
"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.
That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "
Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.
Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.
Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.
"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.

Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.

An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.

Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".
The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.

For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.
"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.
That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.
Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.
Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.
"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

title: The arc of Trump: How the president lost the coalition that put him in the White House
titleJa: The arc of Trump: How the president lost the coalition that put him in the White House
summaryJa: President Trump forged an extraordinary coalition to win office in 2024. A new CNBC survey shows that coalition is now seriously weakened.
bodyOriginal:
President Donald Trump forged an extraordinary coalition to win office in 2024, stitching together his base with unusual support from some traditional Democratic groups like Hispanics and young people. It was enough to sweep the battleground states and catapult him into office for a second term.
The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey shows that coalition is now seriously weakened.
Since the beginning of his second term, the president's net approval rating among Latino voters has dropped from -22 to -38, and declined from -28 to -53 among 18- to 34-year olds. Black respondents have moved from -55 to -67.
Among all registered voters, his approval has fallen from -7 at the start of his term to -19 in the most recent survey.
The decline in the president's approval carries over into the Republican base. Approval from self-described Trump voters has fallen from a net +85 in 2025 to a net of +65. Net approval has even turned negative in the South, from +2 in 2025 to -20 in the latest survey.
The results of the latest poll show why Republicans are facing an uphill battle in the midterm elections next week. Trump is not on the ballot — but his presence will be felt.
Read the full survey results here.
To be sure, Republicans in the survey still give the president an 82% approval rating, and those who say they identify with the MAGA movement are at 90%. But interest in the election is 10 points lower among Republicans than it is for Democrats, and in tight races, the party that better turns out its voters will have an advantage.
The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide found 44% of respondents say their biggest worry if Republicans control Congress is allowing President Trump to operate beyond his constitutional power. By contrast, 28% say their biggest worry for Democratic control is passing policies of Democratic Socialists. For either party's control, registered voters worry that Congress won't do enough to bring down prices.
The survey was conducted Oct. 14-18, and was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies. It carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.
As a second-term president who had skipped four years between terms, Trump's arc of approval has followed an unusual path. The president left office above water on the economy, with 48% approving and 41% disapproving — high numbers for a president whose last year was overwhelmed by the Covid pandemic.
But there was no second-term honeymoon. Trump was immediately underwater in his economic approval rating in the April 2025 CNBC survey. That could have reflected immediate public discontent with the tariff regime and resulting market turmoil. The president's economic approval rating remained negative through most of his first year.
The bottom dropped out, however, with the launch of the Iran war. By April 2026, the president's net economic approval rating was plying depths last seen under President Joe Biden amid the aftermath of the pandemic, when the country was facing high inflation and elevated unemployment.
In the first quarter of this year, Trump's net economic approval dropped 10 points to -21. It has plunged to -31 in the latest survey. Economic disapproval rose to 65%, the highest for any president CNBC has measured back to President Barack Obama, and one point higher than Biden's worst showing. The survey shows increasing disapproval of Trump's handling of inflation. Over the same time, shooting of Americans by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers began to dominate headlines, eroding support for one of the president's major policy initiatives.
The survey this quarter appeared to pick up growing frustration with a host of issues, from immigration to the economy, among those demographic groups that had supported the president in unusual numbers in 2024, with sharp declines in economic and overall approval among Latinos, young people and those in the $50,000 to $75,000 income group.
Most ominously for the president, views on the economic outlook fell 22 points for Republicans. Though still net positive, it was the lowest level of economic optimism for Republicans since Biden.
These downbeat views on the economy do not automatically translate to votes for Democrats. The survey showed a 7-point preference for Democratic control of Congress, a 3-point gain from the July survey. While Republican economic pessimism grew, so did their preference for a Republican-controlled Congress, from 85% in July to 87% in October.
Blue-collar workers show how the president has maintained his base amid growing concern about the economy. Their net economic approval of the president has plunged 22 points to -15 from the beginning of Trump's term to now. But their overall presidential approval remains +6, just a four-point drop. They still prefer a Republican-controlled Congress by 21 points, though that is down from 33 points in July.
The days and weeks leading up to the election have seen the president barnstorming through red states, a sign of concern with the base's enthusiasm. But it also creates the possibility that he could fire up his base and bring them out to stanch potential Democratic gains.
The survey shows that the extra votes from the coalition that put Trump in the White House in 2024 would be a reach for Republican congressional candidates in 2026.

title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
titleJa: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
summaryJa: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
bodyOriginal:
Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
- Published
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.
The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.
Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.
In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.
It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.
Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.
Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
- Published2 hours ago
'Bold but sane'
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.
Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".
Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.
Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.
It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.
However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.
Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.
The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.
'Significant milestone'
Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.
"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.
Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".
He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.
Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?

- Published7 days ago

title: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
titleJa: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
summaryJa: An S&P 500 index without AI stocks is beating the traditional index. These sectors and stocks could be winners if the AI trade keeps fraying.
bodyOriginal:
A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.
A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.
Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.
Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.
Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.
Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.
AI trade loses steam
The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.
Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.
Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.
Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.
Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.
Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.
Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.
Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.
Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

title: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion
titleJa: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion
summaryJa: Meta plans to raise $95 billion to fund AI infrastructure and superintelligence, as Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom eye up to $5 billion in shares.
bodyOriginal:
Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in AI infrastructure and superintelligence.
The stock was up 1.6% in premarket trading after the announcement. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement.
The tech giant will initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.
The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure buildout. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.
Meta's planned investments will support "emerging AI opportunities" including its family of apps, its AI agent Muse and its data center business, the company said Monday.
It plans to balance funding for these investments through a mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and equity capital.
Meta racing to secure AI infrastructure
Meta is among the major hyperscalers that are increasingly tapping debt to fund the expensive infrastructure required for the AI boom.

title: Neocloud stocks fall as Elon Musk says more than 200 of them face 'guppy-level death'
titleJa: Neocloud stocks fall as Elon Musk says more than 200 of them face 'guppy-level death'
summaryJa: Investors are already questioning the debt-fueled expansion of neoclouds and whether the large AI infrastructure build-out will generate long-term returns.
bodyOriginal:
Shares of major neocloud stocks fell on Monday after Elon Musk said that more than 200 companies in the sector could collapse.
Nebius, CoreWeave and Iren all dropped more than 4% in early premarket trading, adding pressure to a sector already facing investor concerns about debt-fueled expansion and whether the large AI infrastructure buildout will generate returns. However, these stocks have since pared some of the losses. Nebius is roughly flat while CoreWeave and Iren are down around 2%.
"As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, said on a post on X on Sunday.
"That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many," he added.
Musk's SpaceX operates its own data centers through which it sells computing capacity. SpaceX is a direct competitor to the neoclouds which also rent compute.
Musk was replying to a post on X by Chamath Palihapitiya, the founder of Social Capital, who laid out his views on the state of the data center buildout. He suggested that there will be "a lot of partially stranded compute and compute sitting in inventory in 2027 than is currently forecasted," which will be "bought and paid for but effectively underearning (below total cost of capital) or collecting dust."
"2027 will be a turbulent year because it will clear out a bunch of wrong/bad bets. It will also be a consolidation year for a few," Palihapitiya said.
Neocloud stocks have taken a hammering over the past month, with CoreWeave and Nebius down more than 30% while Iren has tanked 40%. The sell-off started earlier this month after the spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps hit levels generally viewed as signs of distress. The yields on CoreWeave's bonds also climbed.
Investors have grown jittery over companies that are borrowing heavily to fund the purchase of expensive Nvidia chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Nvidia, neoclouds defend demand
Nvidia, an investor in several neoclouds, looked to shore up the sector last week at its GTC event in Berlin, Germany.
In an interview with CNBC, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the demand for neoclouds is "off the charts."
"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," Huang said.
"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved," he added.
Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, distanced his company from concerns surrounding CoreWeave, saying "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are," in an interview with CNBC. Boroditsky said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. And there could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028.
Iren Co-CEO Daniel Roberts also defended demand.
"We understand the increased focus from investors, but when we're talking from customers, nothing has changed. The demand is still there," Roberts told CNBC last week.
"Next year, we are having conversations with customers covering multiples of all the capacity we possibly bring online, and in the last month or so, 2028 is now coming into focus. But the demand is there," he added.

title: Cracking AI trade has Wall Street looking for a hedge. An ex-Citadel quant may have the answer
titleJa: Cracking AI trade has Wall Street looking for a hedge. An ex-Citadel quant may have the answer
summaryJa: Jasper Zhang runs Hyperbolic, a GPU exchange building a software for "physical" AI futures
bodyOriginal:
As CoreWeave shares plummet, taking much of the AI complex with it, investors face a simple question: what's the best way to hedge AI risk?
An ex-Citadel quant might have the answer.
Jasper Zhang is an ex-Citadel Securities quantitative researcher who now leads Hyperbolic. It's a 50-person financial technology startup building a spot marketplace for tradable GPU computing power, a tool that would allow traders to hedge against a decline in AI demand.
The platform allows investors to buy and sell GPU clusters, the units that power AI compute. This is done through Hyperbolic's Forge software, which virtually logs into clusters worldwide and makes technical tweaks so that mismatched clusters work better together, allowing traders to not just buy and sell a standardized unit of compute, but also control the underlying GPUs for their own purposes.
Zhang says it's as good as being in the data center itself, and sees the technology as the first building block of "physically" settled GPU futures, which, upon settlement, would offer contract owners complete control over a cluster with known characteristics. In other words, it would allow investors a new way to hedge against a decline in AI demand by trading the hardware itself.
Currently, GPU architecture varies wildly depending on how they are assembled, leading to various levels of output. Every data center is different. Networking, memory, and security all affect GPU performance. At the same time, financing agreements often prevent builders from sharing prices, meaning a survey-based index may average setup costs while missing outlier expenses.
In the futures world, that's called "basis risk." It's a problem for market-makers to solve, and a void Zhang hopes Hyperbolic can fill.
The 31-year-old Zhang came to America with several Chinese math medals and finished a math doctorate at U.C. Berkeley in just two years before taking a job at Citadel Securities building trading models. Hyperbolic's head of finance, Hong Chan Kim is a hedge fund veteran, having worked at Point72, Balyasny Asset Management and Citadel LLC, the hedge fund.
Hyperbolic has raised $20 million since its launch in 2022, is in the midst of another funding round, and expects a $150 million annualized run rate by year-end. As of today, the company says it has about 250,000 users and an estimated $200 million worth of annual GPU compute connected to its platform.
Emerging market
Other big players see a similar opportunity in the marketplace for AI hedging tools.
CME Group plans to offer a cash-settled futures product that is tied to GPU pricing maintained by Silicon Data, an index-provider backed by DRW, one of the biggest prop-trading firms in Chicago.
"There's a ton of demand and capital flowing into this ecosystem so there's a lot of risk," Don Wilson, founder and CEO of DRW, said in a call. "Cash futures are a great first building block. There are plenty of electricity futures that are cash-settled, oil futures that are cash-settled, so I think you can start these things either way."
The CME product is currently under review with the CFTC, but the commission recently extended that review period to November 9th, likely also tying up another futures contract proposed by Intercontinental Exchange and data-provider Ornn, backed by Andreessen Horowitz's a16z crypto fund.
"Our guess is when the cash-settled futures come out they're not going to be reflective of what's going on in reality," says Hyperbolic's Kim. "Physical usage is what will tether that connection between the reality and the derivatives."
The bigger issue is that cash futures are an imperfect hedge for real-world risk. If AI demand hits a wall, AI rent-a-centers like CoreWeave could end up sitting on billions of dollars in AI hardware with little to no way to cash out.
"Indices are a normalized global number," said Carmen Li, CEO of Silicon data and DRW-backed Compute Exchange, a marketplace for buying and selling GPUs that is also laying groundwork for physically-settled futures. "You get financially hedged, but if you're looking for procurement, that's not going to help you."
What the AI complex needs most – in particular smaller startups that don't have the capital or credit to risk making big hardware purchases – is a virtual pipeline to physical hardware, contends Zhang.
"CoreWeave's debt situation would be less concerning if providers had more ways to monetize available GPU capacity during a slowdown, especially when long-term contracts carry thin margins," said Zhang. "Cash-settled futures can help falling prices, but they do not by themselves put idle GPUs to work."

title: Trump says he'll soon decide whether to ‘make a deal’ with Iran or ‘finish it off'
titleJa: Trump says he'll soon decide whether to ‘make a deal’ with Iran or ‘finish it off'
summaryJa: Trump said he is weighing a deal with Iran against renewed military action as tensions escalate across the Middle East.
bodyOriginal:
U.S. President Donald Trump has said he was deciding whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off" as investors weigh heightened tensions across the Middle East.
"Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? It's getting to be decision time," Trump said in a Fox News interview on Sunday.
Mediators from Qatar, which has played a key role in efforts to negotiate an agreement between Washington and Tehran, visited Tehran on Sunday, per Reuters. It comes as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia continued over the weekend.
The last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 1. Trump previously said strikes would not resume until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Tehran says it is preparing a military response to any U.S. attacks.
A potential U.S. target could be Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site linked to Iran's nuclear program, Trump said in the Sunday interview.
"We can read the badge on somebody's shirt from space, okay? We know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe Mountain. We know the other three [nuclear sites] are obliterated," Trump said.
Trump also repeated the claim that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global trade and a major flashpoint in the conflict, citing that crude oil flows have returned to pre-war levels.
Energy prices nonetheless remain elevated amid the disruption and a global refining squeeze.
Washington and Tehran have both repeatedly claimed they control the route, where overall trade flows remain severely curtailed, impacting consumer prices.
A Singapore-flagged container ship sank in the strait earlier this month after being struck by an unidentified projectile and catching fire.
Iran Revolutionary Guard navy chief Ali Ozmaei said earlier this month that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships.
Regional powers seek Iran talks
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are meeting Iran's leadership in Tehran on Monday
The three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, committing to closer defense cooperation and stipulating that an armed attack against one member would be regarded as an attack against all.
It is the first meeting of the group since Houthi missiles and drones targeted sites across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh airport and an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco.
Saudi Arabia last week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference until 2027 due to security concerns after a string of fatal strikes.

title: Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital
titleJa: Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital
summaryJa: The deal further advances Apollo Global's ambitions in Abu Dhabi, often called the "capital of capital."
bodyOriginal:
Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Company, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.
The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi, often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.
Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Company, first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.
In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.
For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering over $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.
John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.
"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.
Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.
Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.
Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.
Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

title: Salon owners urge Budget VAT cut as staffing pressures grow
titleJa: Salon owners urge Budget VAT cut as staffing pressures grow
summaryJa: Marcus Perkins, who owns a hair and beauty salon in Brierley Hill, says he is scared for the future.
bodyOriginal:
Salon owners urge Budget VAT cut as staffing pressures grow
- Published
After 22 years running a salon, Marcus Perkins says he is increasingly worried about the future of the hair and beauty industry.
Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to employ staff and invest in apprenticeships, he says, while more salons are turning to self-employed models to survive.
"Seeing salons close on the high street is very scary," he said. "I'm very scared myself. Luckily it hasn't happened yet but who knows what the future holds?"
Perkins is among more than 2,000 salon owners who have signed an open letter calling on the Chancellor John Healey to cut VAT on hair and beauty services from 20% to 10% in this week's Budget.
The letter is backed by the British Hair Consortium (BHC), which argues rising business costs are placing increasing pressure on traditional salon employers.
However, the industry has also seen growing numbers of stylists move into self-employed arrangements, with hairdressers often renting a chair within a salon rather than being directly employed.
With salon ownership perceived to be out of reach for many, self-employment offered independence, flexibility and higher earnings, industry research suggested, external.
A Treasury spokesperson said hair and beauty businesses played an important role in supporting jobs, apprenticeships and thriving high streets.
They added that the sector had benefited from reforms to business rates.
While traditional salons said they faced rising pressures, a recent report from the British Beauty Council found that hair and beauty salons and shops made up almost a third of all leisure sites across UK retail centres.
It added that those businesses now accounted for greater share of smaller high streets and were equivalent to pubs, bars and cafes combined.
There were 50,400 VAT or PAYE registered hair and beauty salons in the UK as of March 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics, external. That compared to 49,300 in March 2024.
Salon owners say they have also been affected by increases in wage, pension and National Insurance (NI) costs.
The government's changes to employers' NI contributions and increases to the minimum wage have been defended by ministers as part of wider efforts to improve pay, support public services and drive economic growth.
The BHC said a reduction in VAT would help businesses take on more staff, invest in training and keep more salons trading on the high street.
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
- Published10 hours ago
Perkins believed it would make a significant difference.
"We can grow the business and employ more people," he said.
The salon owner runs M&M Spa in Quarry Bank, near Brierley Hill, where he says he has trained more than a dozen young people over the past two decades.
Among them is 21-year-old stylist Trearna Hart, who said many of her peers had struggled to establish careers after leaving college.
She said she was fortunate to find an employer willing to invest in her development.
This year alone, Perkins said he had spent about £2,000 on courses and travel costs to support her training.
"It's upsetting really," he said. "We help people, we train, we nurture, we mentor. We help the next generation because if we don't help the next generation, what happens to our future?"
The BHC claimed apprenticeship numbers had fallen sharply and warned the trend could worsen if pressures on employer-run salons continued.
Financial pressures and concerns over inconsistent training standards had led salons to take on fewer apprentices, with 53% of salon owners reporting a reduction, external in the number they trained, according to a Future of Hairdressing report.
Perkins believes businesses that employ and train staff are increasingly competing against models centred on self-employed workers.

title: Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
titleJa: Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
summaryJa: Changes are needed to prevent the full, flat-rate state pension becoming liable for income tax after it rises in April.
bodyOriginal:
Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
- Published
Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.
The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April. This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made.
The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. Healey will explain this pledge will be met by plans for a new tax allowance for low-income pensioners.
Healey's plans come as the Conservatives and Reform UK unveil their alternative Budget proposals, including deep cuts to the welfare bill.
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
- Published10 hours ago
An insider's guide to Budget Day: 'Don't fall off the kerb'
- Published6 hours ago
The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.
More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.
The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.
Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.
The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.
Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.
Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".
The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.
Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.

title: Brazil's Lula wins historic presidential election; Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede
titleJa: Brazil's Lula wins historic presidential election; Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede
summaryJa: It's the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the final runoff after losing in the first round.
bodyOriginal:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil's president, overturning a first-round deficit to beat Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff that split the country almost evenly.
Lula took 51.8% of valid votes to Bolsonaro's 48.2%, according to the Superior Electoral Court, with nearly all ballots counted on Sunday.
The results are also historic as it's the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the final runoff after losing in the first round.
Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, saying he would seek the annulment of the outcome, Reuters reported. He also said a ruling by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting for two hours was "unacceptable," according to the report.
The election process was marred by allegations of voter suppression, with Lula's campaign reporting suspended public transportation in some key areas, prompting the court to extend voting by two hours. Bolsonaro's campaign had also requested an extension, citing heavy rains that shut polling stations in the south, a right-wing stronghold.
The victory of the 80-year-old leftist, who had trailed in the first round, blocks a rightward shift in Latin America that U.S. President Donald Trump has backed.
Trump, who had labeled Bolsonaro's lead in the first round as "a very, very big victory," would have preferred a Brazilian in closer alignment to U.S. foreign policy as Washington makes efforts to project U.S. power across the Americas, according to Daniela Portella Sampaio, senior research fellow for Latin American Security at the U.K. think tank Royal United Services Institute.
Lula, who has publicly sparred with Trump, is set to govern from 2027 to 2030, facing a Congress where Bolsonaro's Liberal Party holds the largest bench in decades, and with a substantial public debt that he would need to stabilize.
Brazil, under Lula's leadership, has grappled with worsening fiscal health and mounting public debt driven by double-digit interest rates, elevated cost of servicing the debt, and rigid mandatory spending. Gross debt reached 82.9% of the country's GDP in August, the highest since March 2021, according to the Central Bank of Brazil.
Markets bracing for rout?
Investors are bracing for heightened volatility across Brazilian markets on Monday following Lula's victory as the right-wing Bolsonaro was seen as more likely to push for fiscal austerity and deregulation.
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) plunged nearly 20% in overnight trading following election results.
Analysts had expected a rally in Brazilian assets before Sunday's election results, with Bolsonaro holding a narrow lead earlier this month. Chris Turner, Global Head of Markets and Regional Head of Research for UK & CEE at ING, had forecast both the currency and bond markets to rally if Bolsonaro won.
The new president will need to convince investors that Brazil can stabilize its debt trajectory, said Alejo Czerwonko, a fellow at the Atlantic Council. Lula's administration will likely extend the more "gradual approach," building on the existing fiscal framework while seeking to preserve public investment and social spending, Czerwonko said.
Goldman Sachs analysts expect "modest measures" to contain the government's spending growth, alongside further increases in an already high tax burden, while major structural reforms remain unlikely.
Leaders from across Latin America largely congratulated Lula's historic win.
Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in a post on X late Sunday, hailed Lula's victory, calling it a "democratic day" for the Brazilian people. Uruguay President Orsi Yamandu congratulated Lula over a call, calling the Brazilian president a "friend."
Lula's victory came the same day as Serbia's long-serving strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat in a parliamentary election to the student-led opposition movement, ending 14 years of leadership.
— CNBC's Matthew Tan contributed to this report.

title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
titleJa: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
summaryJa: What is the Budget and what could be in it?- Published
bodyOriginal:
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
- Published
Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.
He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".
But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited.
Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT.
What is the Budget?
In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes.
Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future.
What might be in the Budget?
The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.
Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.
The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:
Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament
To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament
In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.
Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. While a rise in government borrowing costs will increase debt interest payments, higher inflation could push up tax revenues.
KPMG believes the government's buffer could have fallen to £12bn, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates it could be £20bn.
There has been speculation over what specific measures will be announced in the Budget.
Bank taxes
Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.
The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.
Your First Home scheme
Further details on the Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.
The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.
There were concerns raised that the threshold for eligibility for first-time buyers could be set at £90,000 for a combined income outside London, and £110,000 in the capital, which could have excluded couples such as teachers and nurses, or police officers.
But that threshold is will now be £110,000 outside of London, and £140,000 in the capital, the BBC understands.
Capital Gains Tax
There had been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. However, this has now been ruled out.
Support for pensioners
Pensioners on low-incomes are expected to be shielded from income tax through a new personal allowance. The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. But the full state pension is set to rise above the current £12,570 threshold, meaning about one million people would have needed to pay tax.
Tax on businesses
The Times has reported, external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.
The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.
He is also planning support for small breweries.
Fuel duty
Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.
Healey told the BBC in late September that the time and place for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.
Energy bills
Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276.
There has been speculation, external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.
Mansion tax
The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the mansion tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.
There had been speculation that the government was considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. However, reports now suggest, external Healey has ruled this out.
Cutting red tape
Healey has said the government plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m.
Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.
Social and affordable housing
Healey is expected to add another £1bn to the £39bn planned spend on social and affordable housing in England over the next decade.
Devolved spending
Regional bodies and mayors in England will be given greater powers over spending, starting with £285m next year for things like housing, transport and High Streets. In future the regions will be able to borrow to spend more on local priorities.
What are opposition parties saying?
Opposition parties have released their alternative budget proposals.
The Conservatives are urging the chancellor to reduce spending and borrowing, as well as to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.
Reform UK are recommending that the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.
How is the economy doing?
In the first three months of the year, the UK's economy grew by 0.6%, while in the April-to-June quarter it grew by 0.5%.
The most recent data showed the economy grew by 0.1% in August after growth of 0.4% in July, with both figures stronger than expected.
Analysts say the UK economy is proving resilient in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran.
Energy prices jumped after the conflict led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and gas trade.
Economists expect UK growth to slow in the months ahead as those costs continue to weigh on households and businesses.
Prices for goods and services are still rising faster than wanted. Inflation hit 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.
The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% for the sixth time in a row in September, but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.
What time is the Budget and what happens afterwards?
The Budget speech usually starts at about 12:30 UK time - after Prime Minister's Questions - and lasts about an hour.
It will be broadcast live on the BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website.
The Leader of the Opposition, Conservative MP Kemi Badenoch, will respond to the speech in the House of Commons.
MPs debate the measures for four days, before voting on them.
If approved by MPs, tax changes can come into effect immediately.
However, the government must pass a finance bill to make them permanent.

title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says
titleJa: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says
summaryJa: Elon Musk said in an X post that SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase GPUs.
bodyOriginal:
Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems.
In a post on X on Sunday, Musk said SpaceX had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses.
In a follow-up post, he added that the financing, primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, is expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027.
Bloomberg reported earlier, citing people familiar with the matter, that SpaceX was in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to purchase Nvidia chips.
The proposed financing would use a special purpose vehicle to keep the debt off SpaceX's balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit ratings, according to Bloomberg.
Goldman Sachs was leading talks with investors, including Apollo Global Management, over the financing structure, according to Bloomberg.
The financing underscores the enormous capital requirements of the AI boom, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.
SpaceX has expanded aggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as "Super Intelligence," or SI.
The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release.
Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.
He predicted that more than 200 so-called neocloud companies, which provide cloud computing infrastructure specifically designed for artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads, would face widespread failures and consolidation, with only a small number surviving.
